en: The training in vowels and consonants is established in the sequence of the *repha* and its reverse, as well as in the sequence of the humble and the impassioned; a short vowel followed by a semi-vowel (*ral*) or a sibilant (*ūṣman*) is subject to elision, except for the nasal *ṅ*.
In the repetition [of the word], the number three is expressed by *tri*, excluding the forms *tisṛ* and *tṛ*; [the words] *riṇan*, *śritaḥ*, *ripuḥ*, *krimiḥ*, *kriviḥ*,
*vriśaḥ*, *riśādasaḥ*, *triviṣṭi*, *triṣṭubh*, *jātasya*, *tripadī*, *astra*, *tris*, *tridhātu*, and *tritaḥ*.
In the case of *śrī*, *strī*, *prayoktṛ*, *yastriṃśat*, *krivi*, *rādi*, and so forth, it is with a prefix (*sopadā*).
Then, *riṣaḥ*, *riṣataḥ*, *riśyaḥ*, and *śritaḥ* are without a prefix (*anupadā*), excluding the seven [cases].
Also, when *yakāra* follows, and when *riśa* is uttered at the beginning, *ripuḥ* is without a prefix.
"riṇagniṣṭam," "ririkṣāṃsaḥ," "rihate," and "atha riśādasaḥ"—thus has been stated the entire consonant; now the vowel is being spoken.
(5) Thus ends the first section.
If, in the past, there were even a single *repha*, or if there was no *vikrama*, nor the *anusvāra* or *ṛ*-kāra, that [consonant] has a clear vowel;
and when followed by a conjunct (*saṃyoga*), it is the first [consonant] in the conjunct, with a consonant as its preceding element (*upadha*).
Excluding the consonant, there are three syllables for the name of one who laughs; 2.
When a word ending in a consonant stands before the syllable *so* (s), the vowel that follows it becomes the vowel of the number [indicated by] the letter *ya*, excluding the neuter genders. 3.
"Ā, *sva*, *sa*, *dme*—these are recited as three; thus there are twelve vowels (*svaras*).
And those others which follow consonants (*vyañjana*) and are ambiguous, they too are vowels.
Thus ends the second section. 2.

Because of the contingency of [the substitution of] *vivṛtti* and so forth in cases such as *anuloma*, the rapidity (*kṣaipratā*) would not be obtained in the repetition; thus it is said, "in the three sounds.
Furthermore, in examples such as *riṇanti* and *ekaḥ*, the presence of the letter *r* is certain because of the root *vṛñ*.
Arimṛdha, cararipu, daurṇā, mātkrivi, and aśvinā;
Krivi, daśavriśa, and the divine one; O destroyers of enemies, protect the mortal from the harm of the harmful; may he not perish, for Gaurī is established upon him.
In examples such as *pravobhriyan*, according to the rule *riṅ śayagliṅkṣu*, the substitution of *riṅ* occurs;
thus, from the root *riṣ* (to injure), the form *reṣaṇam* is derived. From the root *ic* (to desire), with the suffix *kvip*, we have *icchā*.
In the phrase *sāvekācastṛtīyādiḥ*, the vowel *e* bears the udātta accent.
"Because of the traditional teaching that *r* and *l* are identical, the *repha* [the sound *r*] is applied to the *kakubha*s.
Thus ends the third section.

Regarding the vowel at the beginning of the *vivṛtti* and so forth, the *repha* occurs by way of *anuloma* and other such applications; and due to the pervasiveness of the *vaṅgr̥da*, there are three conjunctions (*saṃyoga*), as follows: 1.

The perfected one (siddha) utters "garmeti" because the [usual] etymological derivation (*prakṛti*) is untenable; he utters "gṛdeti," for the root *gaṛd* means "to desire. From *gaṛda*, *vaṃśṛda*, and *stṛbhiḥ*—derived from *tṛṇāti*, *tṛṇoti*, and *ṇāstṛta*—it is like the word *akṛta*. 2. From *stṛbhiḥ*, *tṛṇāti*, *tṛṇoti*, and *ṇāstṛta*, it is like the word *akṛta*.

Because of the certainty [of the rule] "that which is increased by conjunction" (*saṃyoge vṛddham*) and so forth in words such as *vardhana*, and because of the force of the comparison with the tree *tṛṣya*— which is a name for a swift [tree]—
the *vṛka*s and others are explained as being "opened" (*vivṛta*) through the emission of light and so forth.
Thus ends the fourth section:

[concerning] all *upadha* vowels followed by a sonant consonant; when a *repha* (the letter *r*) follows a *rephin* (a vowel), those are the *repha-sandhis*. When a *repha* arises, the preceding long *upadha* is shortened.
Both of these are optionally fixed:

the *visarjanīya* followed by a voiced consonant and not preceded by *repha* becomes *ā*; and *o* preceded by a short vowel becomes [a vowel]. These two are the fixed and the optional euphonic combinations (*sandhi*). 2.
The *ninṛti* does not step [there], nor does the anusvāra follow that rule; it is refined by the seasons (*ṛtu*) and the subsequent conjunction (*saṃyoga*). 3.1.67. *vṛṃgada*. *Saṃskṛta*.
Regarding the rule "when there is a prior conjunction, [the vowel] has a consonant as its penultimate," why is it not desired in the case of *nariṣyama kadā cana*?
This is the fifth section. [The verse continues:
*ā susadma nṛṣu yad anne prācā*.
When food goes among men, it destroys the tongue; the three splendors of the pervasive one are scattered even as the path of the wind is spread upon the earth— he who is our food.
"Blazing with wind, O most powerful one, go toward Vṛtra!"— with this twelve-syllable *nṛṣvara* chant, he should recite the second half-verse, "The hero whose body is heated."
O King, when you see him cooked, O Agni,
let this one not be [consumed];
as the seven-fold sound of the cooked [offering] resounds, like a wolf or a deer in the *ka*-group of consonants.
In the *Ṛgveda*, they desire the *ṛ* sound in the *avitra* [section] and in the word *agni-guḥ*;
likewise, in the *Cavarga* [section], they desire it in *ṛcā* and in *ṛju-riñjase*. 4–5.
Thus, when a consonant is obscured by the repetition [of vowels],
as in *mṛra* for *ṛṇāni* and *ririg*, the *repha* (the sound *r*) is accumulated; and in the *tavarga*, as in *ṛtam vṛthādād udareṇa*.

In *ṛṣak tritaḥ*, the *repha* (the sound *r*) is elided when followed by a semivowel (*antasthā*). In *ajāgṛj jāgṛviṃ triviṣṭidhā dvit*, the *repha* is elided because it serves the purpose of expressing a number.
In "yuṣmāsu ṛṣyaḥ riśādasaḥ," the *ṛ* is combined with the *repha*;
in "ṛṣṭayo riṣam," the *ṛ* is [combined] with the *repha*. 8.

The great Bṛhaspati belongs to Bṛsaya; that which begins with *ka*, *pa*, and *ca*—namely the semi-vowels (*antasthā*) *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*—is the external consonant beginning with *ka*. Thus ends the sixth section.
Having completed the training in vowels and consonants.
